text.p: Yesterday's crash of an MD11F cargo jet operated by Federal Express in Newark looks as if, at $115 million, it will be the most expensive aviation insurance loss so far this year. The plane was a complete write-off. It was a relatively new aircraft and therefore expensive. No one died.

All this adds up to a reminder ahead of the autumn renewal season of what airlines are paying their insurance premiums for. The FedEx loss will provide underwriters with a lever to try to argue up rates, which have been falling from a cyclical high for around five years.

However, realistically, underwriters know that the loss of one cargo aircraft, even an expensive one, is not going to turn the tide. It would probably take several major aviation incidents involving heavy loss of life to push rates.

In stark contrast, there were two major passenger aircraft losses last year -- a Valujet in Florida and flight TWA800 in New York. Insurance claims from these two are still being negotiated and will overshadow the account for the year.
Passenger liability claims for the Valujet loss are expected to top $200 million, while the figure for the Paris bound TWA flight could go much higher than that.

Faced with falling rates and growing risk potential as jets become bigger, London based aviation insurers have been steadily giving ground in a market they used to dominate and still often lead. Others are more than willing to step in and accept business at the lower rates, despite the warnings of seasoned underwriters that it is only a matter of time before a combination of incidents wipes out the premium base.
Just how much chance is involved in this was demonstrated by the FedEx crash. FedEx's aviation insurance account renews on August 1. What a difference a day will make to some insurers.
